extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, and patent practitioners drafting claims for improvements (U.S. practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting patent claims that cover improvements over prior art, with emphasis on whether to use Jepson-format claims and how to avoid admissions that limit claim scope. Focused on U.S. claim-drafting practice and prosecution risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify advantages over the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing you must do is figure out what the advantages are over the prior art. You need to take a critical look at your own invention and identify that which distinguishes it over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about distinguishing features; analyze examples (e.g., hitch-mounted toilet seat: paper holder and collection canister distinguish the later patent). This analysis drives what to claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on structure, not method of use
rubrics_metrics.description: You should absolutely focus on structure, not on the method of use. Differences in the method of use will only come into play if you are claiming a new and nonobvious method of using, which is typically not the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In majority of cases protect the device/apparatus (structural features); don't rely on use-differences unless you are claiming a distinct method claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. 1.75(e) Jepson claim template (regulatory guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: (e) Where the nature of the case admits, as in the case of an improvement, any independent claim should contain in the following order: (1) A preamble comprising a general description of all the elements or steps of the claimed combination which are conventional or known, (2) A phrase such as 'wherein the improvement comprises,' and (3) Those elements, steps, and/or relationships which constitute that portion of the claimed combination which the applicant considers as the new or improved portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the CFR-referenced template describing Jepson-format claims. The article notes the rule but warns against following it blindly; use only where truly appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Jepson claims in most circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming done as Rule 75(e) suggests is known as writing a claim in Jepson format ... No patent attorney in their right mind would follow this suggestion. A Jepson claim is not something that you must employ and it comes with significant disadvantages with only the most nuanced of advantages that present in a very rare circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jepson claims create admissions and limitations that can harm claim scope and prosecution options. The author strongly recommends avoiding Jepson claims except in rare, specific situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making admissions — prosecution history estoppel risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything you do say can and will be used against you FOREVER! This relates most directly to what is known as prosecution history estoppel. When you make an argument to a patent examiner or make certain amendments or responses you are forever prevented from undoing what you did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not characterize elements as 'known' or concede aspects of the prior art unnecessarily. Build prosecution strategy without premature admissions; let counsel manage arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson preamble elements are treated as prior art / claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When using the format of Rule 75(e) the preamble is considered to positively and clearly include all the elements or steps recited therein as a part of the claimed combination. Therefore, the elements or steps recited in the preamble become a part of the claim and do in fact act as limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Jepson format is 'taken as an implied admission that the subject matter of the preamble is the prior art work of another' (MPEP 2129). This can expand the universe of prior art considered against the claim and limit scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft claims positively with proper antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive introductions avoid admissions. Example claim (from '860 patent) shows each piece introduced separately with proper antecedent basis (i.e., 'a' or 'an' the first time introduced and 'the' or 'said' when subsequently discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write claims in traditional format with clear antecedent basis, introducing elements neutrally (no statements that elements are 'known' or part of the prior art). This preserves flexibility and avoids inadvertent admissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson format can trigger means-plus-function interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Jepson claim meet means plus function claiming! Means plus function claiming is not evil per se, but is far more nuanced than inventors and newbies are ready to handle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: Jepson structure and terse descriptions of the improvement may lend themselves to means-plus-function analysis, which imposes additional limitations (e.g., limiting scope to corresponding structure in the specification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson may be appropriate to overcome double patenting (rare exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: One such situation where it may be appropriate to use a Jepson claim is when the patentee is attempting to overcome, or prevent, a double patenting rejection. ... when the patentee employs the Jepson format to avoid a double patenting rejection over the patentee's own work, the use of the Jepson format causes no deleterious effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only consider Jepson when distinguishing the patentee's own foundational work (not treated as prior art in the same way) or when an examiner suggests it; analyze carefully and consult counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson claims can and should be rewritten into traditional format
rubrics_metrics.description: There is absolutely no reason why a Jepson claim could not be re-written into traditional format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, re-draft improvements in traditional claim format that avoid admissions and state elements positively. See linked drafting guides for basic claiming and method claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not self-represent on claim format choices; consult trained professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors who seek to represent themselves beware! ... Jepson claims should be avoided in all but rare circumstances. Leave Jepson claiming to the trained professionals. Please do not attempt this at home!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Jepson and claim-format choices have long-term, potentially irreversible prosecution consequences, seek experienced patent counsel rather than DIY drafting.
